title: $p$-Form Gauge Dynamics and Digital Quantum Simulation -- Flux and Cosmological Constant Neutralization
abstract: I develop a Hamiltonian framework for ${\mathbb Z}_k$ $p$-form gauge fields on arbitrary oriented cell complexes in arbitrary dimensions. Gauge qudits are defined by $p$-cells, charged boundary qudits by $(p-1)$-cells, Gauss-law generators by boundary map $\partial_p$, and magnetic checks by $\partial_{p+1}$. The same cellular structure produces local dressed Wilson operators, and at $k=2$ a Calderbank-Shor-Steane check complex relevant to quantum error correction. I then specialize to $p=2, k=2$, where the magnetic 3-cell term is absent and the one-form Gauss-law can be solved exactly. The physical Hilbert space is parameterized by plaquette electric-flux variables, while the link configuration is reconstructed as the dynamical boundary of the evolving flux domains. The reduced Hamiltonian is an Ising-type plaquette model, where its local transverse-field term is the physical image of the boundary-dressed Wilson operator $σ_p^z\prod_{\ell\in\partial p}τ_\ell^z$. A tube-cap quench compares two initial flux fillings with the same initial boundary loops. Exact diagonalization on $4\times4$, $6\times4$, and $5\times5$ tori finds that the cap loses $20$-$37\%$ of its occupied-flux area, while the tube remains nearly pinned. A finite-size scaling locates a dynamical crossover of tension-to-density ratio near $(m/\varepsilon_E)_c\simeq1.89$. The unreduced plaquette-plus-link encoding provides local Gauss-law checks and a direct digital implementation, while the reduced plaquette-only Hamiltonian supplies the exact benchmark. The result places the specific top-form discharge and the cosmological constant neutralization calculation inside a general higher-form Hamiltonian and coding framework.
summary: This paper constructs a Hamiltonian framework for $p$-form gauge fields on lattices, modeling phenomena relevant to cosmology. By simulating 'quench' dynamics on specialized plaquette Hamiltonians, the authors observe distinct decay behaviors between different initial flux configurations. The results establish a quantitative crossover point and place top-form discharge within a general higher-form theoretical structure.
main_problem: Developing a Hamiltonian framework for $Z_k$ $p$-form gauge fields to study flux dynamics, which has implications for cosmological constant neutralization.
main_result: The simulation shows that in a 'tube-cap quench,' the cap loses 20–37% of its occupied-flux area while the tube remains nearly pinned, and a dynamical crossover is located near $(m/\epsilon E)_c \simeq 1.89$.
method: Exact diagonalization (ED) on tori combined with numerical simulations analyzing time evolution under quench protocols.
model_or_system: The model uses $Z_k$ $p$-form gauge fields defined on arbitrary oriented cell complexes, specialized to a plaquette-only Ising-type Hamiltonian after solving the one-form Gauss law. This structure is compared against redundant link-plus-plaquette encodings.
key_observables: Occupied-flux area ($M(t)$), boundary length ($L(t)$), and the contrast $\mathcal{M}_{	ext{cap}}(t) - \mathcal{M}_{	ext{tube}}(t)$.
important_parameters: The ratio of boundary energy to electric flux ($\epsilon E$) versus link tension ($m$), with a critical crossover point near $1.89$.
main_assumptions: The link occupation is treated as a derived observable determined by adjacent plaquette fluxes, not an independent variable.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the time evolution of occupied-flux area and decay rates across parameter sweeps on tori, pinpointing crossover regimes.
paper_structure: The work builds from general $p$-form gauge theory to a specialized, reduced plaquette Hamiltonian suitable for ED. It then applies this framework to quench dynamics simulations, comparing results between the simplified model and the full digital encoding.
why_interesting: The study of flux dynamics in lattice gauge theories provides rich non-equilibrium physics analogous to phase transitions or relaxation processes studied in classical statistical mechanics models.
